### /docs/components/Form/Listbox

Listbox documentation page — standardized structure

Listbox Listbox presents a list of options where the user can select one or more. Unlike a dropdown, options are always visible — no opening required. Supports filtering, icons, and multi-select. What, When & Why What is it? A visible list of selectable options with keyboard navigation (arrows, Home/End, type-ahead). Options can contain rich content (icons, descriptions). When should I use it? Use <Listbox> for 5–15 options that benefit from being always visible. For fewer options, use radio buttons. For hidden-until-opened options, use <Select> or <Combobox> . Why does it exist? Always visible — no dropdown to open; all options scannable at a glance. Rich content — options can include icons, avatars, descriptions. Keyboard accessible — full arrow key navigation, Home/End, type-ahead. Sources WAI-ARIA APG — Listbox Primer — ActionList Twintrinsic Implementation Always-visible list of options (no dropdown to open) `filter={true}` enables a filter input for narrowing options `filterPlaceholder` for the filter input placeholder text WAI-ARIA listbox pattern with `role="listbox"` + `role="option"` Form context integration via `getContext('form')` Common Mistakes Don't use for fewer than 5 options — use radio buttons or checkboxes Don't forget `aria-selected` on the selected option Related Components Select, Combobox, AutoComplete, Menu Responsiveness Fills container width; scrollable when options overflow. Touch targets meet 44×44 px minimum. Customization Single or multiple selection. Filterable via filter= . Option icons via optionIcon . Wrap with <FormField> for labels and validation. Examples Basic Usage `}> Multiple Selection `}> With FormField `}> Disabled `}> With Filter `}> Props Events Accessibility Uses role="listbox" and role="option" . aria-selected on selected options. Arrow keys, Home/End, type-ahead navigation. Visible focus indicators. Keyboard Support Key Function Arrow Up / Arrow Down Navigate between options Home / End Move to first/last option Enter / Space Select highlighted option Type Jump to matching option

NumberInput NumberInput is a specialized form control for numeric values with increment/decrement buttons, currency/percentage formatting, and unit suffixes. What, When & Why What is it? A text input restricted to numeric values with up/down stepper buttons, optional prefix/suffix (e.g., "$", "%", "°C"), and configurable decimal precision. When should I use it? Use <NumberInput> when the user needs to enter or adjust a specific numeric value: quantity, price, percentage, temperature. For approximate values on a continuous range, use <Slider> instead. Why does it exist? Precision — stepper buttons and keyboard arrows allow exact values. Formatting — built-in currency, percentage, and unit display. ### /docs/components/Form/Radio

Radio documentation page — standardized structure

Radio Radio is a form control for selecting exactly one option from a small set of mutually exclusive choices. It wraps the native <input type="radio"> with consistent styling and accessibility enhancements. What, When & Why What is it? A circular toggle that, when selected, deselects all other radio buttons in the same named group. All options are always visible — the user doesn't need to open a dropdown to see choices. When should I use it? Use <Radio> when the user must choose exactly one option from a small set (2–6 options). All options should be visible for faster scanning. For 7+ options, use <Select> or <Combobox> . For independent on/off toggles, use <Checkbox> or <Switch> . Why does it exist? Visibility — all options are visible at once, enabling faster decision-making than dropdowns (Nielsen Norman Group research). Mutual exclusion — the name attribute ensures exactly one option can be selected per group. Keyboard intuitive — arrow keys navigate between options in a group, matching user expectations. Slider Slider is an input for selecting a value or range from within a given minimum and maximum. It supports horizontal and vertical orientations, tick marks, tooltips, and multiple visual variants. Intuitive — the spatial metaphor (left = less, right = more) is universally understood. Efficient — one drag gesture covers the full range faster than typing. Accessible — follows WAI-ARIA slider pattern with arrow key support. ### /docs/components/Form/Switch

Switch documentation page — standardized structure

Switch Switch is a toggle control that switches between on and off states. It is visually styled as a sliding track with a thumb, and semantically distinct from a checkbox — it represents an immediate state change rather than a form value. What, When & Why What is it? A binary toggle with a sliding animation. Unlike a checkbox (which represents "checked" or "unchecked"), a switch represents "on" or "off" — the semantics communicate that the setting takes effect immediately. When should I use it? Use <Switch> for settings that activate/deactivate something immediately: dark mode, notifications on/off, auto-save, airplane mode. Use <Checkbox> for form values that are submitted with the form (e.g., "I agree to terms"). Why does it exist? Better semantics — screen readers announce "on/off" instead of "checked/unchecked", which is clearer for settings. Visual metaphor — the sliding track communicates instant effect better than a static checkbox. Platform familiarity — switches are the standard toggle pattern in iOS and Android settings. Sources WAI-ARIA APG — Switch MDN — switch role Primer — ToggleSwitch Material Design 3 — Switches Ant Design — Switch Twintrinsic Implementation Uses `<input type="checkbox" role="switch">` — native checkbox with switch semantics Screen readers announce "on/off" instead of "checked/unchecked" CSS transition on the track for smooth sliding animation `accent-color` for brand-tinted track color Form context integration via `getContext('form')` Common Mistakes Don't use `<div role="switch">` — always `<input type="checkbox" role="switch">` Don't use for form values — use Checkbox for checked/unchecked semantics Related Components Checkbox, FormField Responsiveness Switches are inline elements that sit naturally alongside their labels. Touch targets meet 44×44 px minimum for mobile tap areas. Use size prop ("sm", "md", "lg") for different contexts. Customization Size: sm , md (default), or lg . For label-less switches, use ariaLabel for screen readers. Theme colors (track, thumb, focus ring) are controlled by the Tailwind theme. Examples Basic Usage `}> With Initial Value `}> Different Sizes `}> Disabled States `}> Required Field `}> Without Label Airplane mode `}> Airplane mode Slots The Switch component does not expose named slots. Use props for customization. Props Events Accessibility Uses a native <input type="checkbox" role="switch"> for maximum compatibility. Screen readers announce "on/off" instead of "checked/unchecked". Visible focus indicators with sufficient contrast. Labels properly associated via for / id . High contrast between track and thumb colors. Textarea Textarea is a multi-line text input for collecting longer text content — descriptions, messages, comments, or any content that spans more than one line. A multi-line text field that handles line breaks, scrolling, and resizing natively. The autoResize prop enables CSS-based auto-grow behavior using field-sizing: content — no JavaScript required. When should I use it? Use <Textarea> whenever the user needs to enter more than one line of text: product descriptions, comments, messages, bio fields, address lines. For single-line input, use <Input> instead. Why does it exist? Native handling — the <textarea> element natively handles line breaks, text wrapping, and resizing. Auto-grow — field-sizing: content (CSS) auto-expands the field to fit content without JavaScript. Consistency — ensures all textareas share the same label positioning, error display, and focus styling. ### /docs/components/Lazy/Lazy

Lazy documentation page — standardized structure

Lazy Lazy renders its content only once it scrolls into the viewport, using an IntersectionObserver . Use it to defer off-screen content and keep initial page loads fast. What, When & Why What is it? A deferral wrapper that uses IntersectionObserver to mount content only when it becomes visible. Supports a placeholder snippet shown during the loading state. Falls back to immediate rendering when IntersectionObserver is unavailable. When should I use it? Use <Lazy> for below-the-fold content: charts, heavy components, or anything that doesn't need to be in the initial paint. For panel-level lazy loading, use <LazyPanel> . Why does it exist? Performance — reduces initial page weight. Scroll-triggered — content mounts when visible. Graceful fallback — immediate render when observer is unavailable. Sources MDN — IntersectionObserver web.dev — content-visibility Primer — Blankslate Ant Design — Skeleton W3C — IntersectionObserver Twintrinsic Implementation Intersection Observer for viewport detection `<img loading="lazy">` for native image lazy loading `content-visibility: auto` for off-screen content skipping LazyPanel variant for tab panels Common Mistakes Don't use JS timers for lazy loading — Intersection Observer is the standard Don't forget `content-visibility: auto` as a CSS-only alternative for simple cases Related Components Skeleton, Card, Container Responsiveness Fills container width by default. Placeholder content adapts to the container. Customization placeholder snippet — content shown while loading. Custom rootMargin to start loading before the element is visible. Examples Basic Lazy Monthly revenue chart Only rendered once it scrolls into view. `}> Monthly revenue chart Only rendered once it scrolls into view. With Placeholder Loading chart… Live analytics widget Deferred until visible. `}> Loading chart… Live analytics widget Deferred until visible to keep the page fast. Props Accessibility Falls back to immediate rendering when IntersectionObserver is unavailable. Loading state exposes aria-live="polite" and aria-busy . Deferred content is only mounted when visible. Keyboard Support Lazy is a behavior wrapper and does not require keyboard interaction. Deferred content maintains its native keyboard behavior once mounted.

### /docs/components/LocaleSwitcher/LocaleSwitcher

LocaleSwitcher documentation page — standardized structure

LocaleSwitcher LocaleSwitcher is a language picker that switches the active Paraglide locale. It renders either a group of toggle buttons or a native <select> , and each language is shown in its own script (e.g. "Español", "فارسی") so every option stays readable no matter the active locale. What, When & Why What is it? A small component backed by the Paraglide runtime's getLocale / setLocale . Switching a locale uses the cookie strategy (the same one this docs site uses), so the page reloads in the new locale and the server re-renders every message via m() . The onchange event reports the new locale if you need to react client-side. When should I use it? Whenever your app uses Paraglide and needs a visible locale control — a header, settings page, or a floating demo-site pill like the one on this docs site. Pair it with getTextDirection() from the Paraglide runtime to flip the document direction for RTL languages. Why does it exist? Self-naming locales — each language names itself, so the control works before a message is even resolved. Accessible — the button group uses the toggle-button pattern ( aria-pressed ) and the select is a native element. Copy-friendly — it's a pattern component: drop it into your app, adjust the locales union, and it works with your Paraglide setup. Paraglide Setup LocaleSwitcher imports from $lib/paraglide , the output directory Paraglide generates. Wire the Vite plugin and a project.inlang/settings.json exactly like this repo: Keep the locales in sync with your message files. The component's LocaleCode union should match them too. Examples Buttons `}> Select `}> Custom Locales `}> Custom Label `}> Props Events Accessibility The button group exposes role="group" with an aria-label , and the active locale is marked with aria-pressed (toggle-button pattern). The select variant is a native <select> with a label and aria-label , so it works with any screen reader for free. Focus rings are visible on every control, and the group is a single keyboard tab stop (arrow keys move between buttons). Keyboard Support Key Function Tab Focus the locale group or select → / ↓ Move to the next locale button ← / ↑ Move to the previous locale button Enter / Space Activate the focused locale

Why does it exist? Leaflet integration — battle-tested, lightweight mapping library. Custom CRS — pixel-based coordinates for custom image maps. Event system — click, zoom, and move handlers for interactivity. Tile providers — OpenStreetMap, CartoDB, and more. ### /docs/components/Masonry/Masonry

Masonry Masonry creates Pinterest-style grid layouts with items of varying heights. It provides responsive, dynamic layouts that automatically adjust to different screen sizes and content dimensions. What, When & Why What is it? A JavaScript-based masonry layout engine that positions items of varying heights into columns, always placing the next item in the shortest column. Uses ResizeObserver and MutationObserver for dynamic content. When should I use it? Use <Masonry> for image galleries, card grids, dashboards, or any layout where items have different heights. For uniform-height grids, use CSS Grid. Why does it exist? Variable heights — CSS Grid/Flexbox can't natively do true masonry. Responsive — breakpoint-based column counts. Dynamic — auto-positions items when content changes. Re-layouts on container resize via ResizeObserver . Customization columns — fixed number or responsive breakpoints object. gap — gap between items in pixels. columnWidth — fixed column width (overrides columns ). centered — center the grid. animated — animate item positions. ### /docs/components/Menu/Menu

Menu documentation page — standardized structure

Menu Menu displays a list of actions or options in a dropdown panel. Uses popover="auto" for light-dismiss and top-layer stacking, with CSS Anchor Positioning for viewport-aware placement. What, When & Why What is it? A button that opens a dropdown menu containing clickable items. Items can include icons, dividers, submenus, and keyboard shortcuts. When should I use it? Use <Menu> for action menus (edit, delete, share), context menus (right-click), or navigation menus (settings, account). For value selection from a list, use <Select> or <Listbox> . Why does it exist? Popover API — light-dismiss, top-layer, and Esc-to-close with zero JS. WAI-ARIA menu pattern — arrow keys, Home/End, type-ahead, focus trapping. Rich content — items can have icons, descriptions, shortcuts, and submenus. Touch targets meet 44×44 px minimum. Customization Trigger content via trigger snippet. Menu content via content snippet. Icons, dividers, disabled items, and submenus on each MenuItem. Examples Data-Driven Menu Instead of using <MenuItem> sub-components, you can pass a flat array of item objects. ### /docs/components/Menu/MenuItem

MenuItem documentation page — standardized structure

MenuItem is a sub-component of Menu . See the parent component docs for usage, examples, and full API reference. MenuItem MenuItem represents a single item within a Menu. Items can be links, buttons, active, disabled, or have nested submenus. What, When & Why What is it? A clickable list item inside a Menu dropdown. Renders as a link (if href is set) or a button. Supports icons, dividers, and nested submenus. When should I use it? Always inside a <Menu> component. Each action or navigation option gets its own <MenuItem> . Why does it exist? Semantics — role="menuitem" announces correctly to screen readers. Consistency — shared styling, spacing, and focus behavior for all menu items. Accessibility — keyboard navigation handled by the parent Menu. Responsiveness Touch targets meet 44×44 px minimum. Text truncation on overflow. Customization Icon via icon prop. Divider before item via divider prop. Disabled state via disabled prop. Active state via active prop. Nested submenu via value + children . Examples Basic Items Options Edit Copy Delete `}> Options Edit Copy Delete Props Accessibility role="menuitem" on all items. Links use native <a> ; buttons use native <button> . Disabled items use aria-disabled . Submenus have aria-haspopup .

AreaChart documentation page — standardized structure

AreaChart AreaChart — An SVG area chart for displaying trends over time with filled areas. Supports single and multiple data series with optional stacking. What, When & Why What is it? An SVG area chart for displaying trends over time with filled areas. Supports single and multiple data series with optional stacking. When should I use it? Use AreaChart for showing trends over time where the filled area emphasizes volume (e.g. website traffic, revenue over time). For simple line trends, use LineChart. For categorical comparison, use BarChart. Choosing the Right Chart Chart Best For Avoid When AreaChart Volume emphasis, cumulative totals, stacked comparisons Multiple overlapping areas make it hard to read LineChart Trends over time, comparing multiple series, showing rate of change Need to emphasize total volume; data is categorical BarChart Categorical comparison, discrete values, ranking Time-series with many data points (too many bars) PieChart Part-to-whole (fewer than 7 slices) More than 7 categories; comparing similar values Use Cases Daily active users — AreaChart (emphasizes volume of users) Revenue breakdown by product — Stacked AreaChart (cumulative contribution) Temperature over time — LineChart (simpler, less visual weight) Storage usage over time — AreaChart (shows capacity filling up) Why does it exist? SVG rendering — crisp at any resolution. Multi-series — stacked or overlapping areas. Interactive — hover tooltips and click events. Responsive — adapts to container size. Sources MDN — SVG WAI-ARIA APG — Data Visualization D3.js — Area Charts Chart.js — Area Charts Ant Design — Area Chart Twintrinsic Implementation SVG-based chart rendering for Area, Bar, Line, Pie, Donut, HorizontalBar `aria-label` on chart container for screen readers Accessible data tables as alternatives `content-visibility: auto` for off-screen charts Common Mistakes Don't use `<canvas>` without a text alternative — SVG is more accessible Don't forget to provide an accessible data table alternative Related Components KPICard, MetricGrid, GaugeChart Responsiveness Fills container width by default. SVG charts scale to any resolution. Customization Custom colors, labels, and sizes. Grid lines, legends, and axis labels. Examples `}> Stacked AreaChart `}> Props Accessibility SVG elements include proper ARIA roles and labels. Color contrast meets WCAG AA standards. Legend provides text alternative to colors. Keyboard Support Chart components are display-only elements. Interactive data points support focus via Tab and activation via Enter/Space.

Dashboard Examples Comprehensive examples showing how to build data dashboards using Metrics components. ### /docs/components/Modal/Modal

Modal documentation page — standardized structure

Modal Modal displays content in a native HTML <dialog> element that requires user attention. It uses closedby="any" for built-in light-dismiss (Escape, backdrop click, and platform close gestures), native focus management with an inert background, and @starting-style entry/exit animations — no manual focus trap, backdrop div, or Escape listener. What, When & Why What is it? A dialog overlay built on the native <dialog> element. It renders in the top layer, manages focus automatically, and traps keyboard interaction within the dialog. The closedby="any" attribute gives native light-dismiss (Escape + backdrop click + platform close gestures like the mobile back button). When should I use it? Use <Modal> for critical tasks that require the user's full attention: confirmations (delete, discard), forms that must be completed before continuing, or displaying detailed information that shouldn't be mixed with the page content. For non-blocking notifications, use <Toast> . For inline expandable content, use an Accordion. Why does it exist? Native <dialog> — built-in focus management, inert background, and light-dismiss. closedby="any" — native Escape, backdrop click, and platform close gestures with zero JS. Entry/exit animations — @starting-style + transition-behavior: allow-discrete for smooth transitions. CSS :has() — prevents body scroll while open without body-class bookkeeping. Content slides open/closed with Svelte's slide transition. When should I use it? Use <Panel> for content that can be collapsed to save vertical space: FAQ sections, settings panels, advanced options, or collapsible documentation. For always-visible content, use <Card> . For layout wrapping, use <Container> . Why does it exist? Space saving — collapse less-used content to reduce page length. Progressive disclosure — show details on demand. Keyboard accessible — toggle with Enter/Space via native button. Smooth animation — slide transition for expand/collapse. ### /docs/components/Progress/Progress

Progress documentation page — standardized structure

Progress Progress displays a progress bar using the native HTML <progress> element. It provides consistent styling, accessibility features, and various display options for showing progress towards a goal. What, When & Why What is it? A progress indicator built on the native <progress> element. It communicates the completion status of a task, upload, or multi-step process. Supports determinate (known percentage) and indeterminate (unknown duration) modes. When should I use it? Use <Progress> when you can quantify completion (file upload at 72%, form 3 of 5 steps). For unknown-duration operations (searching, loading), use indeterminate . For page-load placeholders, use <Skeleton> . Why does it exist? Native <progress> — built-in role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow / aria-valuemin / aria-valuemax . Variants — semantic colors (success, warning, error) convey status. Indeterminate mode — CSS-animated bar for unknown-duration tasks. ### /docs/components/PropsTable/PropsTable

PropsTable A utility component that renders a component's props as a documentation table. It reads the props directly from a component module that exports propsMetadata , or renders a data hash as a fallback. If neither is available, it logs a console.warn . Usage Auto-derived props Pass the component module (namespace import) to render its propsMetadata export: Explicit data hash When a component doesn't export propsMetadata , pass a plain data hash of prop name → descriptor: Props Accessibility Uses a semantic <table> with header cells for each column Prop names and types are rendered in <code> for clarity The table scrolls horizontally on narrow viewports instead of overflowing

### /docs/components/Sidebar/Sidebar

Sidebar documentation page — standardized structure

Sidebar Sidebar is a collapsible vertical navigation panel that attaches to the left or right edge of its parent container. It provides a persistent home for nested navigation links, filters, settings, or secondary content — and collapses to a hamburger-triggered overlay on mobile. What, When & Why What is it? A vertical panel with an optional header snippet, scrollable body content, and a collapsible toggle. It can be positioned on the left (default) or right side, and supports two mobile modes: float (overlay with backdrop) and inline (push content). When should I use it? Use a Sidebar when your app has 5+ top-level navigation items, deeply nested navigation hierarchies (admin panels, documentation sites), or persistent secondary content (filters, settings panels) that should remain visible while the user works. Why does it exist? Hierarchical navigation — vertical lists accommodate nested items better than horizontal tabs or top bars. Discoverability — always-visible navigation reduces the number of clicks/taps needed to reach deeply nested pages. Accessibility — uses <nav aria-label> so screen-reader users can jump directly to sidebar navigation. Sources WAI-ARIA APG — Landmarks MDN — <nav> Primer — NavList Material Design 3 — Navigation rail Responsiveness Desktop (≥ 640 px) — the sidebar is visible and pushes or overlays main content, depending on the mode prop. Mobile (< 640 px) — the sidebar collapses and reappears as a slide-in overlay with a backdrop when toggled. Touch targets meet the 44×44 px minimum for mobile tap areas. Customization Position: left (default) or right . Mode: float (overlay) or inline (push content). Custom header via the header snippet. Theme colors, borders, and spacing controlled by the Tailwind theme. Examples Basic Sidebar A left-positioned sidebar that fills the full height of its container, with navigation links. Supports nested hierarchies and search. ### /docs/components/Skeleton/Skeleton

Skeleton documentation page — standardized structure

Skeleton Skeleton displays loading placeholders while content is being fetched. It provides various shapes and sizes to match different content types and includes smooth CSS-native animations via @starting-style . What, When & Why What is it? A placeholder component that mimics the shape of the content it replaces during loading. It uses a shimmer animation to signal that content is incoming, giving users a visual indication of layout structure before real data arrives. When should I use it? Use <Skeleton> when content is loading asynchronously and you want to preserve layout stability (no content shift). Combine multiple skeletons to match the shape of cards, lists, or articles. For known-duration operations, use <Progress> instead. Why does it exist? Layout stability — prevents content shift (CLS) during loading. Perceived performance — users see structure instead of blank space. CSS-native animations — shimmer via @starting-style and CSS keyframes, no JS. Rendering performance — content-visibility: auto for off-screen skeletons. Sources MDN — CLS Material Design 3 — Skeleton Primer — SkeletonLoader Ant Design — Skeleton web.dev — content-visibility Twintrinsic Implementation CSS `@keyframes` shimmer animation with `@property` for gradient angle `@starting-style` for smooth entry animation `content-visibility: auto` for off-screen skeleton performance `aria-busy="true"` and `aria-live="polite"` on the loading region `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` for exit when content loads Common Mistakes Don't use spinners for layout-heavy content — skeletons show structure Don't forget `aria-busy="true"` — screen readers need loading state Related Components Progress, Lazy, Toast Responsiveness Width defaults to 100% , filling its container. Circle variant uses a fixed size prop (48px default). Text variant auto-wraps to container width. Customization Variants: text , rectangle , circle , rounded . Custom width, height, and border radius. Multi-line text via lines prop. Disable animation with animated= . Examples Basic Skeleton `}> Variants `}> Rectangle (default) Circle Rounded Text Multi-Line Text `}> Loading Pattern (Card) `}> Static (No Animation) `}> Props Accessibility Uses role="status" to announce loading state to screen readers. Includes aria-label to describe what is loading. Provides visually hidden text for screen reader users. Skeleton elements are marked with aria-hidden="true" when appropriate. Keyboard Support The Skeleton component is a static display element and does not require keyboard interaction. It communicates loading state to assistive technology via ARIA attributes.

### /docs/components/Splitter/Splitter

Splitter Splitter creates a resizable divider between two adjacent containers, allowing users to drag and adjust the width or height of each panel. It is ideal for layouts like code editors, file explorers, or any interface that needs flexible space allocation. What, When & Why What is it? A two-panel layout with a draggable divider that follows the W3C APG window-splitter pattern . The divider uses role="separator" , tabindex="0" , and aria-valuenow/min/max for full keyboard and screen reader support. When should I use it? Use <Splitter> when users need to adjust the relative size of two panels: code editor + preview, file tree + content, inbox + message view. For simple side-by-side layouts without resizing, use CSS Grid or Flexbox. Why does it exist? User control — let users customize their workspace layout. Keyboard accessible — arrow keys for fine control, per W3C APG. Persistent — storageKey saves the split position in localStorage. Constrained — min/max size prevents panels from collapsing. ### /docs/components/Stepper/Stepper

Stepper Stepper displays progress through a sequence of logical and numbered steps. It is commonly used for multi-step forms, wizards, or any process that requires users to complete steps in a specific order. What, When & Why What is it? A sequential navigation component that shows the user's current position in a multi-step process. Each step can be completed, active, pending, or in error. Supports horizontal and vertical orientations with optional step content display. When should I use it? Use <Stepper> for workflows with 3+ sequential steps: checkout flows, registration wizards, onboarding sequences, or configuration steps. For tabbed content that can be accessed in any order, use <Tabs> . Why does it exist? Progress visibility — users always know where they are in the process. Linear and non-linear modes — enforce sequential steps or allow free navigation. Vertical and horizontal orientations — adapts to different layout contexts. Error state — clearly marks failed steps for user attention. ### /docs/components/Stepper/StepperStep

StepperStep documentation page — standardized structure

StepperStep is a sub-component of Stepper . See the parent component docs for usage, examples, and full API reference. StepperStep StepperStep is an individual step within a <Stepper> . It renders a numbered (or icon) marker, a title, an optional subtitle, and — for vertical steppers — the step's content when active or expanded. Steps derive their completed/active/pending state from the parent <Stepper> 's activeStep , or from their own explicit props. What, When & Why What is it? A single step within a <Stepper> container. It manages its own visual state (completed, active, pending, error, optional, disabled) and renders the step marker (number or custom icon), label, optional subtitle, and content area. When should I use it? Always use <StepperStep> inside a <Stepper> . Each logical step in your process gets its own <StepperStep> . Why does it exist? Self-contained state — manages completed/active/pending/error per step. Context-driven — inherits state from the parent Stepper when not explicitly set. Rich content — supports custom icons, subtitles, and inline content. Sources Material Design 3 — Steppers Ant Design — Steps Primer — Stepper WAI-ARIA APG — Tabs MDN — aria-current Responsiveness In horizontal mode, steps compress and labels may wrap on narrow screens. In vertical mode, content is full-width and naturally responsive. Alternative labels stack below icons on small viewports. ### /docs/components/Timer/Timer

Timer documentation page — standardized structure

Timer Timer displays a countdown or count-up with optional pause, resume, and reset controls. It pairs a large monospace readout with one of three display variants — a Progress bar, a GaugeChart, or a KPICard — so the same timing logic can back anything from a toast countdown to a Pomodoro session. What, When & Why What is it? A self-contained timing component that counts down from a duration or counts up toward one. It fires update events on every tick, fires a complete event when the duration is reached, and can loop automatically. The readout is a live role="timer" region backed by a visual variant. When should I use it? Use <Timer> whenever you need visible, controllable time: toast auto-dismiss countdowns, media or presentation timers, focus sessions, count-up trackers (time on task), or step-limited flows. When the progress is secondary to a number, prefer the bar variant; use gauge for a single-goal readout and kpi when the remaining time belongs in a dashboard card. Why does it exist? Consistent timing — one tick loop with pause/resume/reset semantics shared across display variants. Accessible — the readout uses role="timer" so assistive tech can query the remaining time. Composable — onupdate / oncomplete callbacks wire into toast dismissal, analytics, or state. Deterministic — fixed 100&nbsp;ms ticks keep drift negligible without depending on rAF timing. Responsiveness Centered column layout that scales down to small widths; the readout uses tabular-nums so digits never jitter. The bar variant is constrained with max-w-sm ; gauge and KPI sizes come from the size / card layout. Control buttons meet the 44&times;44 px touch target minimum. Customization Modes: countdown (default) or countup . Variants: bar (Progress), gauge (GaugeChart), kpi (KPICard). Colors: primary , secondary , success , danger , warning , info . format accepts a custom formatter; label titles the display. showControls toggles the built-in buttons; loop restarts on completion. running externally controls the countdown (e.g. pause on hover); omit it for self-managed timing via autoStart and the buttons. showReadout hides the large time display for bar-only embedding (as used inside Toast). Examples Basic Countdown `}> Count Up `}> Display Variants `}> Loop `}> Custom Format (milliseconds / 1000).toFixed(1) + "s"} />`}> (milliseconds / 1000).toFixed(1) + "s"} /> Without Controls `}> Props Events Accessibility The readout uses role="timer" with aria-live="off" semantics — screen readers announce it on demand instead of being spammed every tick. Control buttons carry explicit aria-label s that flip between "Pause timer" and "Resume timer" so the current action is always announced. The KPI variant is keyboard-operable ( role="button" , Enter/Space toggles pause/resume). Focus rings are visible on all controls. Keyboard Support Key Function Tab Move focus between the pause/resume and reset buttons Enter / Space Activate the focused control (pause/resume or reset) Enter / Space on the KPI card Toggle pause/resume

### /docs/components/Toast/Toast

Toast documentation page — standardized structure

Toast Toast displays temporary, non-blocking notifications. Entry/exit animations use pure CSS ( @starting-style + transition-behavior: allow-discrete ) with no JavaScript animation logic. The container uses content-visibility: auto for rendering performance. What, When & Why What is it? A lightweight notification component that appears temporarily to inform users of an action's result. Toasts auto-dismiss after a configurable duration and can be paused on hover. They are managed via a global store, so any component can trigger them. When should I use it? Use <Toast> for feedback that doesn't require user action: "Profile saved", "File uploaded", "Connection restored". For critical messages that block the workflow until acknowledged, use <Modal> . Why does it exist? Non-blocking — doesn't interrupt the user's current task. Global store — any component can trigger a toast without prop drilling. CSS-native animations — @starting-style and allow-discrete for smooth entry/exit with zero JS. Rendering performance — content-visibility: auto skips off-screen containers. Sources WAI-ARIA APG — Alert MDN — alert role Material Design 3 — Snackbar Primer — Toast Ant Design — Message Twintrinsic Implementation `@starting-style` + `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` for entry animation `content-visibility: auto` for off-screen performance `aria-live="polite"` region for screen reader announcements Auto-dismiss countdown powered by the Timer component (pausable on hover) Multiple toasts stack (not limited by Popover API) Common Mistakes Don't use Popover API for toasts — it's one-at-a-time, conflicts with stacking Don't forget `aria-live="polite"` — screen readers need to announce new toasts Related Components Modal, Skeleton, Progress Responsiveness Max width max-w-sm (384px); collapses on small screens. Positioned in corners or centered; doesn't overlap the viewport edge. Touch targets meet 44×44 px minimum for close button. Customization Variants: default , primary , success , warning , error , info . Positions: top-right , top-left , top-center , bottom-right , bottom-left , bottom-center , middle-left , middle-right . Configurable duration (ms; `0` = persistent), max toasts, dismissible, and pause-on-hover. The auto-dismiss countdown is rendered by the Timer component; `progress: false` hides the bar. ### /docs/components/Tooltip/Tooltip

Tooltip documentation page — standardized structure

Tooltip Displays additional information on hover or focus. Built on the native Popover API ( popover="hint" ), the interestfor attribute, and CSS Anchor Positioning — requiring zero JavaScript for show/hide, positioning, light-dismiss, or accessibility wiring. What, When & Why What is it? A popup that appears when the user hovers or focuses a trigger element. The tooltip renders in the top layer, is positioned automatically via CSS Anchor Positioning, and is light-dismissed by pressing Esc . When should I use it? Use <Tooltip> for supplementary hints — icon labels, button descriptions, truncated text expansion. For rich interactive popups, use <Popover> . For persistent information, use <Modal> . Why does it exist? Zero JS — browser handles show/hide, positioning, and ARIA wiring. Top-layer — never clipped by overflow: hidden ancestors. WCAG 1.4.13 — hoverable, dismissible, persistent (users can move to the tooltip). CSS Anchor Positioning — tethers to the trigger with viewport-edge flipping. Sources WAI-ARIA APG — Tooltip MDN — Popover API Chrome — CSS Anchor Positioning Material Design 3 — Tooltips Twintrinsic Implementation Uses `popover="hint"` + `interestfor` for hover-triggered display CSS Anchor Positioning for tethering to the trigger element `role="tooltip"` + `aria-describedby` on the trigger Escape dismisses; no focus inside tooltip Common Mistakes Don't put focusable content in a tooltip — use a dialog/popover instead Don't forget `aria-describedby` — screen readers need the tooltip linked Related Components Menu, Popover, Modal Responsiveness Tooltip positions automatically adapt to viewport edges via CSS. On touch devices, tooltips are not practical — use a popover or detail expansion. Customization position — top, right, bottom, left. content — text or HTML content. Arrow repositioning via CSS position-try-fallbacks . Examples Basic Tooltip Save `}> Save Tooltip Positions Top Right Bottom Left `}> Top Right Bottom Left How It Works The trigger uses the interestfor attribute to reference the tooltip's ID. On hover/focus, the browser opens the tooltip as a popover="hint" in the top layer. CSS Anchor Positioning ( anchor-name / position-anchor + anchor() functions) tethers the tooltip to the trigger — no getBoundingClientRect() or manual coordinate math. For browsers without native support, the @oddbird/popover-polyfill , @oddbird/css-anchor-positioning , and interestfor polyfills are loaded automatically via loadPlatformPolyfills() . Props Accessibility Automatic ARIA wiring — interestfor sets aria-describedby or aria-details on the trigger. WCAG 1.4.13 — Dismissible (Esc), hoverable (pointer can move to tooltip), persistent. Top-layer rendering — never clipped by overflow ancestors. Mutual exclusion — popover="hint" auto-closes other hint popovers. Arrow repositioning — flips automatically via CSS position-try-fallbacks . Keyboard Support Key Function Esc Close the tooltip Tab Focus the trigger (opens tooltip)

### /docs/components/Tree/Tree

Tree documentation page — standardized structure

Tree Tree displays hierarchical data with expandable/collapsible nodes. Ideal for file explorers, org charts, category navigation, and document outlines. What, When & Why What is it? A nested list of TreeNode elements with expand/collapse controls, selection modes, connecting lines, and full keyboard navigation. Uses role="tree" / role="treeitem" . When should I use it? Use <Tree> when data has a parent-child hierarchy: file systems, org charts, nested categories, document outlines. For flat lists, use a Listbox or Select. Why does it exist? Hierarchical navigation — expand/collapse reveals nested items. Keyboard — arrow keys, Home/End, Enter/Space, type-ahead. Selection — single or multi-select modes. Sources WAI-ARIA APG — Tree View Primer — TreeView Twintrinsic Implementation `<details>` + `<summary>` for expand/collapse — native HTML ARIA treeview pattern: `role="tree"` / `role="treeitem"` / `role="group"` `aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-level` for screen readers Arrow keys: Right expands, Left collapses, Up/Down navigate siblings `multiSelect` implies `selectable` (fixed in recent commit) Common Mistakes Don't use a nested `<ul>` without ARIA roles — tree semantics require `role="tree"` Don't forget `aria-level` — screen readers need depth information Related Components TreeMenu, Listbox, Menu Responsiveness Scrollable when the tree is taller than the container. Icons on individual TreeNodes. Examples Basic Tree `}> Selectable `}> With Lines `}> Expanded by Default Use expandAll to expand every node at once, or set expanded on individual nodes. `}> Multi-Select `}> Data-Driven Tree Use the items prop to render a tree from a data array instead of composing <TreeNode> sub-components. ### /docs/components/Tree/TreeNode

TreeNode documentation page — standardized structure

TreeNode is a sub-component of Tree . See the parent component docs for usage, examples, and full API reference. TreeNode TreeNode is a single node inside a Tree. Renders a WAI-ARIA treeitem with expand/collapse controls, selection, icons, and custom labels. What, When & Why What is it? A collapsible list item within a Tree. Each node can have children (nested TreeNodes), an icon, and custom label content. When should I use it? Always inside a <Tree> . Each item in the hierarchy gets its own TreeNode. Leaf nodes have no children; parent nodes expand/collapse. Why does it exist? Semantics — role="treeitem" with aria-expanded . Consistency — shared expand/collapse behavior and focus styling. Accessibility — keyboard navigation handled by parent Tree. Examples Basic Nodes `}> Expanded and Selected `}> Disabled Node `}> With Icons `}> Props Events Accessibility role="treeitem" with aria-expanded , aria-selected , aria-disabled . Expand/collapse buttons labeled for screen readers. Full keyboard navigation via parent Tree.

### /docs/components/TreeMenu/TreeMenu

TreeMenu documentation page — standardized structure

TreeMenu TreeMenu renders a hierarchical menu as a tree of items. Supports nested menus, links, actions, icons, separators, and integration with the Sidebar component. What, When & Why What is it? A tree-structured navigation menu where parent items expand to reveal children. Each item can be a link, a button action, or a text-only header. When should I use it? Use <TreeMenu> for deep navigation hierarchies: admin panels, documentation sidebars, file explorers. For flat navigation, use a simple <nav> with links. For action menus, use <Menu> . Why does it exist? Hierarchical navigation — expand/collapse reveals nested items. Sidebar integration — passes items directly to Sidebar. Flexible — links, buttons, actions, icons, separators in one component. Twintrinsic Implementation Combines tree semantics with menu behavior Hierarchical navigation items that expand/collapse Uses `role="tree"` / `role="treeitem"` for semantics `...rest` spread for native attributes Common Mistakes Don't use for flat navigation — use Menu or Breadcrumb instead Don't forget keyboard navigation — arrow keys should work like Tree Related Components Tree, Menu, Sidebar Responsiveness Scrollable when the menu is taller than the container. Touch targets meet 44×44 px minimum. Customization Item structure: title / label , icon , link , onClick , children . Separators via separator: true . Nested depth is unlimited. Examples Basic Menu `}> Nested Items `}> With Actions alert('Create clicked') }, , ], }, ] `}> Props MenuItem Structure Property Type Description title string Main label for top-level items label string Alternative label (used in children) icon string Icon identifier link string Navigation href (renders as anchor) onClick () => void Click handler separator boolean Show separator before this item children MenuItem[] Nested menu items Accessibility Semantic HTML with proper link and button elements. Keyboard navigation (Enter to expand/collapse). ARIA labels for screen readers. Focus management for keyboard users.

### /docs/examples/game-map

Game Map Example - Interactive map with markers, popups, and editing

Game Map Example An interactive game map with markers, popups, and editing capabilities. Click on the map to create new markers, click on existing markers to edit them. How It Works This example demonstrates the <Map> component's custom image mode using customImage with imageWidth / imageHeight props. This enables pixel-based coordinates via Leaflet's Simple CRS, perfect for game maps, floor plans, and diagrams. Key Features Custom image overlay — Any image can be used as a map layer. The customImage prop loads the image and maps pixel coordinates to map positions. Interactive markers — Click on the map to create new markers. Each marker type (treasure, enemy, NPC, location) has a unique icon and color. Edit popups — Click a marker to open an edit popup. Modify the name, description, or type. Save or delete directly from the popup. JSON sync — The JSON editor on the right shows all markers in real-time. Edit the JSON directly to update the map, or modify markers on the map to update the JSON. How to Build This Start with the <Map> component and pass your image via customImage . Set imageWidth and imageHeight to match your image dimensions. Use the markers prop to define marker positions using pixel coordinates. Provide a popupContent function to render rich HTML popups with edit forms. Handle onclick to capture new marker positions when the user clicks the map. Use onmarkerclick to handle marker saves, edits, and deletions. Marker Types Type Icon Use Case Treasure 💎 Loot, collectibles, hidden items Enemy ⚔️ Enemy spawn points, boss locations NPC 🧑 Quest givers, shopkeepers, allies Location 📍 Points of interest, landmarks, fast travel Interactive Demo Nexus Mods ' onmarkerclick= onclick= /> Markers JSON } height="100%" /> Edit the JSON to update markers in real-time. Changes are reflected on the map immediately.

### /docs/examples/shopping/guide

Shopping Page A walkthrough of building an e-commerce landing page — hero banner, category navigation, filter sidebar, product grid, and a large multi-column footer — using Twintrinsic components. Hero Header A full-bleed banner with a background image sets the tone for the page. Since the docs layout's main content area has its own padding, the hero breaks out of it with a negative margin that matches that padding exactly ( -mx-5 cancels App 's p-5 ), then restores its own horizontal padding on the inner content. Category Navigation A row of top-level links sits directly below the hero, similar to a retail site's persistent category bar. Each entry is a MenuItem , overriding its default block/full-width styling so it lays out inline in a flex row. Filter Sidebar Checkbox , Slider , and Rating combine to build a typical product-filter panel. None of their value / checked props are two-way bindable by design — update your own state from their onchange / oninput callbacks instead. (sampleChecked = !sampleChecked)} /> ) => (samplePrice = e.detail.value)} /> ) => (sampleRating = e.detail.value)} /> /> (maxPrice = e.detail.value)} /> (minRating = e.detail.value)} />`} Product Grid Each product is a Card with an image prop, a header snippet for the product name, a readonly Rating and price in the body, and a footer snippet holding the "Add to Cart" action. The href prop makes the whole card a real link, and hoverable adds the hover affordance. Wireless Noise-Cancelling Headphones $199.99 Add to Cart Mega Footer Large retail sites often close with a dense, multi-column footer full of department and policy links. The Footer component's center snippet is used to hold a responsive link grid, while its default background/border are overridden to get a deliberately dark band. Best Practices Breaking Out of Layout Padding When a section needs to be full-bleed inside a padded layout, use a negative margin that exactly matches the parent's padding (e.g. -mx-5 for p-5 ), then re-apply your own horizontal padding on the inner content. Controlled, Not Bindable Slider , Rating , and Checkbox are controlled components — pass value / checked down and update your own state from their callback props rather than reaching for bind: . Real Links for Real Cards Passing href to Card renders it as a real anchor element instead of a non-semantic clickable div , giving you free keyboard and screen-reader support. Accessible Placeholder Links Demo footer/category links use href="#" as a stand-in for real destinations. In production, always point links at real routes so they're meaningful to assistive technology and keyboard users.

### /docs/theming

Theming documentation page

Theming Twintrinsic uses CSS variables and Tailwind CSS for theming. You can customize the look and feel of your application by modifying these variables. Color System Base Colors Background --color-background Surface --color-surface Border --color-border Text --color-text Muted --color-muted Color Scales Twintrinsic provides a comprehensive color system with 10 shades for each color scale (50-900). These color scales provide a consistent palette for your application. Text & Background Combinations Here are some common text and background color combinations that provide good contrast and follow accessibility guidelines. Use these combinations for consistent UI elements. + UI Component Examples The color system is applied consistently across all UI components. Here are some examples of how the colors are used in buttons: Customization CSS Variables To customize the theme, override these CSS variables in your stylesheet: Live Theme Customizer Pick base colors below and Twintrinsic generates a full 50-900 scale for each accent, previews real components against the result, and prints a ready-to-copy CSS block. Nothing here is saved or applied to the rest of the site — it's scoped to the preview panel via inline CSS custom properties. Dark Mode Dark mode is supported through the data-theme="dark" attribute on the root element. Customize dark mode colors by overriding these variables: Additional Themes Beyond the default light/dark pair, the Storybook demo environment ships five additional themes (plus a dark variant of each) so you can preview components under different color strategies: a brand-accent theme, a high-contrast theme, and three color-vision-deficiency (CVD) themes. They are demo themes only — they live in .storybook/themes.css and are intentionally NOT part of the shipped library CSS, so consumers of Twintrinsic only get the default light/dark pair. The docs site imports the same file so the Theme Preview page can render them side by side. Themes are selected via the data-theme attribute on the root element. Every custom theme also has a dark variant : append -dark to the theme name (e.g. data-theme="brand-dark" ). The dark: custom variant matches any data-theme value ending in -dark , so dark-mode utilities and tokens engage automatically: data-theme="brand" / data-theme="brand-dark" — a teal/cyan accent palette on teal-tinted surfaces that swaps the default purple identity for a cooler, product-style feel. Every component follows along because they all consume the same --color-primary-* / --color-secondary-* / neutral tokens. data-theme="high-contrast" / data-theme="high-contrast-dark" — a WCAG AAA-leaning theme with pure black text on white (or pure white on black), near-black/white borders, and tuned accent scales so colored text and filled buttons keep strong contrast. Color Vision Deficiency (CVD) Themes Three additional themes (plus dark variants, e.g. data-theme="protanopia-dark" ) are tuned for the most common color vision deficiencies using the Okabe-Ito blue-orange safe-axis strategy — they never rely on red-vs-green or blue-vs-yellow alone, so status colors stay distinguishable in both light and dark: data-theme="protanopia" / data-theme="protanopia-dark" — for red-blind users. Success shifts from green to teal (blue-green) and error shifts from red to vermillion-orange; the orange/amber axis stays readable. data-theme="deuteranopia" / data-theme="deuteranopia-dark" — for green-blind users. Success shifts to cyan (reads as blue) while error keeps a strong red, which is still visible without the green cone. data-theme="tritanopia" / data-theme="tritanopia-dark" — for blue-yellow blind users. Primary becomes magenta, secondary red-purple, warning moves from yellow to orange, and info shifts from blue to teal; success and error keep green and red. The theme switcher in Storybook is a grouped light/dark picker : a Mode dropdown (Light / Dark) plus a Theme dropdown (Default, Brand, High Contrast, Protanopia, Deuteranopia, Tritanopia). Dark + Brand applies data-theme="brand-dark" , and so on for every combination. Both dropdowns are built on Storybook's core globalTypes toolbar mechanism, so there is no addon dependency to manage. You can add your own themes by defining a matching [data-theme="..."] block in src/lib/twintrinsic.css and adding it to the themes map in .storybook/preview.ts . Avoiding the Light-Mode Flash Because theme detection happens in client-side JavaScript, the page can briefly render in light mode before ThemeToggle applies the saved or system-preferred theme. To prevent that flash, add this blocking inline script to your SvelteKit app.html before %sveltekit.head% : Tailwind Configuration The theme is also available through Tailwind CSS utility classes. Here's how to configure your tailwind.config.js : Using Colors in Components When building components, use the Tailwind classes to apply colors consistently. Here are some examples:

### /docs/utilities

Utilities documentation page — shared helper functions exported from the public barrel.

Utilities Twintrinsic ships a small set of shared helper functions used by the Form select family (AutoComplete, Listbox, Combobox) and the group components (TagGroup, ChipGroup). They are re-exported from the package entry point, so you can import them alongside components: All helpers accept an item plus an optional field name used to derive the label or value when the item is an object. Always pass the field name explicitly when your objects use a custom key — the helpers default to "label" / "value". Label Extraction getItemLabel getItemLabel(item, labelField = "label") → string Derives a display label for an item. Primitives are stringified as-is; objects yield item[labelField], with null/undefined field values collapsing to "". This unifies the former per-component ?.toString() || "" label pattern. Value Extraction getItemValue getItemValue(item, valueField = "value") → unknown Derives a comparison/submission value for an item. Objects yield item[valueField]; primitives pass through unchanged. Falsy primitives ("", 0, false, null, undefined) are intentionally not collapsed — so a numeric option 0 survives selection comparison. Group Removal dispatchGroupRemove dispatchGroupRemove(items, index, eventName, handler?) Resolves the item at index from the items array and invokes the group's remove/dismiss callback with a CustomEvent whose detail carries ' ' . Shared by TagGroup ("dismiss") and ChipGroup ("remove"). Language Detection detectLanguage detectLanguage(content: string) → string Heuristically detects a code language from content patterns (HTML, CSS, JavaScript/TypeScript, JSON, YAML, Markdown, Svelte, shell). Used by CodeBlock when no language prop is provided. Documentation Tables PropsTable & EventsTable For rendering component props and events in your own docs, Twintrinsic ships two utility components — PropsTable and EventsTable. They auto-derive their rows from a component module at build time, with an explicit-array fallback. See their dedicated pages for full usage: PropsTable and EventsTable .
